The packet lacks NVIDIA earnings, margin, cash-flow or guidance data, so the $228.38 price (about $5.5 trillion market cap) cannot be checked against fundamentals, and NVIDIA's $6.3 billion CoreWeave backstop adds contingent exposure.

parsed.rationale: The packet shows strong AI demand: hyperscaler capex near $646 billion, H100 rental prices up almost 40%, and capacity booked through September 2026. However it contains no NVIDIA revenue, earnings, margin or cash-flow data, so a fundamental valuation cannot be anchored. At $228.38 and roughly $5.5 trillion market cap, the price implies continued growth that the packet cannot verify. Risks include grid delays pushing capacity into 2027, faster custom-accelerator growth at Broadcom, and NVIDIA's $6.3 billion CoreWeave backstop, which adds contingent exposure. Balancing these, the stock looks fairly valued with low confidence.

Risks are custom-silicon competition, circular financing exposure and physical bottlenecks. Broadcom's AI revenue is growing 221% and guided to $115B for FY27. Nvidia backstops customers such as CoreWeave. Grid delays and packaging and HBM constraints could limit or delay shipments and raise costs.

parsed.rationale: At $228.38 (about $5.5T market cap), the pre-announced quarter implies an annualised data-centre run rate above $400B at 76%+ gross margin. Demand indicators such as hyperscaler capex and rising rental prices support further growth. Offsetting this are the risk that the cycle peaks, as the 2024 rental price decline showed, custom-chip share gains, vendor-financing circularity, and power and supply constraints. I see modest upside to about $265 and rate it attractive, with moderate confidence.

drivers.claim: Earnings power is very strong and accelerating: data-centre revenue of $89.0B (+117% y/y), 75% gross margin, and guidance of $108B total revenue next quarter imply a run-rate of roughly $430B a year. At a ~$5.5T market cap that is about 13x sales, which looks modest if margins hold.

Demand backdrop is robust: hyperscaler capex of about $646B in 2026, plus H100 rental prices up ~40% and capacity sold out, point to a supply-constrained market with pricing power. CoWoS and HBM constraints (HBM ASP +121% in 2027) cap near-term supply, but they support sustained tightness.

Risks temper the upside: custom accelerators are growing fast (Broadcom AI revenue +221%, $115B FY27 guide), vendor-financing and backstop arrangements add circularity risk, power and grid delays could push out deployments, and the 2024 rental price decline shows how quickly cycles can turn.

parsed.rationale: Annualised revenue of roughly $430B at 75% gross margin and 117% data-centre growth suggests earnings well above what a $5.5T valuation implies, and supply-constrained conditions support that. Fair value of about $265 allows for a discount for cyclicality, competition from custom silicon, circular financing exposure and power-grid delays. The upside is moderate rather than large, so the stock looks attractive but not strongly undervalued.

At $40.88 and a market cap of about $16B, the shares already price in much of the contracted ramp. IREN itself warns that the contracted run-rate is not fully contracted and may differ materially. Supply-chain easing in CoWoS and HBM adds some risk.

parsed.rationale: About $4B of contracted annualised revenue, with Microsoft and NVIDIA as anchors, and a tight GPU rental market support the bull case. But only about $1B is live, and FY2026 AI Cloud revenue was only $128.8M. Execution and financing risk remain, and the company cautions that the run-rate may differ materially. At roughly $16B market cap the stock seems to price in much of the ramp, so I rate it fairly valued with low confidence.

Platinum ClusterMAX ranking supports a pricing premium, though the SemiAnalysis and Foreign Policy sources are secondary or commercially interested.

Execution and cash-flow risk is high: only about 1GW of 5GW contracted power is expected to be connected by end-2026, ARR must rise roughly 2.3-3x in H2 2026, GAAP net loss was $190.4M, and 2026 capex guidance is $20-25B, partly offset by customer prepayments on about 70% of deals.

parsed.rationale: Nebius shows strong demand and pricing signals, with ARR guided to $7-9B and deals reportedly above $20M revenue per MW with under two-year payback. However, the stock is priced at roughly 16x 2026 revenue guidance, and reaching ARR targets needs a steep H2 ramp with only about 1GW of 5GW connected. GAAP losses and $20-25B capex add funding and execution risk. The packet lacks balance sheet, debt, and cash data, so a precise fair value is not supportable. Balancing upside from pricing against delivery risk, the shares look fairly valued at about $230 with low confidence.

drivers.claim: Demand and pricing power look strong: GPU rental prices rose sharply through 2026, capacity is reported sold out and booked, and Nebius announced about a 20% rise in one-year reserved contract prices effective October 1, 2026.

Growth is highly execution-dependent: ARR must rise roughly 2.3 to 3 times in H2 2026 to meet the $7 to $9 billion guidance, but only about 1 GW of 5 GW contracted power is expected to be connected by year-end, and the GAAP net loss and $20 to $25 billion capex plan add funding risk.

Unit economics and funding are favourable on paper (over $20 million revenue per MW, payback under two years, and prepayments covering 50 to 60% of capex on about 70% of deals), but the packet gives no net debt, forward earnings or cash flow, so a precise intrinsic value cannot be established against the roughly $52 billion market capitalisation.

parsed.rationale: At $235.88 (about $52 billion market cap on roughly 220 million shares), the packet supports a business with strong demand, rising GPU pricing and attractive per-megawatt economics. However, the 2026 ARR guidance requires a steep second-half ramp, connected power lags contracted power sharply, and capex and GAAP losses are large. Valuation cannot be finished without net debt, forward earnings or cash flow, and the share count is from a single secondary source. Some sources are sponsored or secondary, and the GPU price series differ across items. On balance the shares look roughly fairly valued, with a point estimate of about $225 and low confidence.

Execution risk is high. Only about 1 GW of roughly 5 GW contracted power is expected to be connected by end-2026, and ARR must rise about 2.3 to 3 times in the second half to meet guidance. Guidance could be missed, which would weigh on the valuation.

Demand and pricing are supportive. GPU rental prices rose about 40% from October 2025 to March 2026, capacity is sold out, and Nebius reports deals above $20 million per MW with prepayments covering part of capex. Some sources are secondary or non-independent, which limits confidence.

parsed.rationale: Demand signals are strong: GPU prices are rising, capacity is sold out, and deal economics look attractive. However, the packet does not establish that the current price is cheap. The market cap of about $52 billion sits well above the FY2026 ARR guidance, and the company is loss-making with $20 to $25 billion of planned capex. Only about 1 GW of 5 GW contracted power is expected to be connected by year-end, and ARR must roughly triple in H2 to hit guidance. Without debt, cash, or share count dilution data, the valuation cannot be firmly tested. Fair value is a rough estimate with low confidence.

drivers.claim: Demand far exceeds supply. Data-centre revenue grew 117% to $89.0B at a 75% gross margin, and guidance of $108B implies a run-rate near $430B. On my assumption of a roughly 55% net margin, the $5.5T market cap is only about 23x run-rate earnings.
Tight compute markets support pricing power for now: H100 rental prices rose almost 40%, capacity is sold out through August to September 2026, and CoWoS supply remains short.

Several risks cap the upside and justify a discount: Broadcom's custom XPUs are gaining share, grid delays could push 30-50% of planned US capacity into 2027, HBM cost inflation may squeeze margins, and Nvidia carries financing and backstop exposure.

drivers.claim: Demand for AI compute looks strong: H100 one-year rental prices rose about 40% from October 2025 to March 2026, on-demand capacity is sold out, and hyperscaler capex is estimated at about $646 billion for 2026.

Growth is constrained by supply and deployment, and custom-chip competition is rising: data-centre power delays may push 30% to 50% of 2026 capacity into 2027 or later, Broadcom's AI revenue grew 221% with custom XPUs at 73% of it, and CoWoS packaging gaps persist.

Nvidia's own exposure is a risk: it acts as supplier, equity investor and backstop, with about $2 billion of CoreWeave equity and a $6.3 billion purchase backstop. drivers.claim: Demand signals are strong: H100 one-year rental prices rose about 40% from October 2025 to March 2026, on-demand capacity is sold out, and 2026 hyperscaler capex is estimated at about $646 billion, mostly for AI data centres and accelerators.

Supply and execution constraints limit near-term upside: 30% to 50% of remaining 2026 US data-centre capacity may slip into 2027 or later, and CoWoS packaging is still roughly 10% to 20% short. Competitive pressure is also rising, since Broadcom's custom XPUs now make up 73% of its AI revenue.

Nvidia's balance sheet carries contingent risk from its AI financing role: it holds about $2 billion of CoreWeave equity and a $6.3 billion backstop on unsold capacity, which makes earnings quality harder to assess. The $228.38 close implies a roughly $5.5 trillion market cap, but the packet has no earnings or forward multiples to test it against.
